mechanism_of_action.value: Aspirin is a more potent inhibitor of both prostaglandin synthesis and platelet aggregation than other salicylic acid derivatives. The differences in activity between aspirin and salicylic acid are thought to be due to the acetyl group on the aspirin molecule. This acetyl group is responsible for the inactivation of cyclo-oxygenase via acetylation.

reversal.dose: Activated charcoal slurry within 3 hours of ingestion; IV sodium bicarbonate to achieve urine pH >= 7.5; hemodialysis for severe poisoning
reversal.notes: Treatment consists primarily of supporting vital functions, increasing salicylate elimination, and correcting the acid-base disturbance. After lavage and/or emesis, administration of activated charcoal, as a slurry, is beneficial, if less than 3 hours have passed since ingestion.

refs.quote: Treatment consists primarily of supporting vital functions, increasing salicylate elimination, and correcting the acid-base disturbance. Gastric emptying and/or lavage is recommended as soon as possible after ingestion, even if the patient has vomited spontaneously. After lavage and/or emesis, administration of activated charcoal, as a slurry, is beneficial, if less than 3 hours have passed since ingestion.

refs.quote: Central Nervous System: Agitation, cerebral edema, coma, confusion, dizziness, headache, subdural or intracranial hemorrhage, lethargy, seizures. Fluid and Electrolyte: Dehydration, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis

Pregnant women should only take aspirin if clearly needed. Because of the known effects of NSAID's on the fetal cardiovascular system (closure of the ductus arteriosus), use during the third trimester of pregnancy should be avoided.

lactation_summary.value: Salicylate is excreted in breast milk. High doses may cause rashes, platelet abnormalities, and bleeding in nursing infants; avoid high-dose therapy.

refs.quote: Nursing mothers should avoid using aspirin because salicylate is excreted in breast milk. Use of high doses may lead to rashes, platelet abnormalities, and bleeding in nursing infants.

value.effect: Aspirin inhibits platelet aggregation and can displace warfarin from protein-binding sites, significantly increasing bleeding risk.
value.management: Monitor coagulation parameters (INR/aPTT) closely and assess regularly for bleeding symptoms when coadministered.

refs.quote: Patients on anticoagulation therapy are at increased risk for bleeding because of drug-drug interactions and the effect on platelets.

value.effect: Aspirin inhibits renal tubular secretion of methotrexate, elevating serum concentrations and potentiating bone marrow and mucosal toxicity.
value.management: Avoid concurrent high-dose salicylate therapy with methotrexate; monitor hematologic indices closely.

refs.quote: Salicylate can inhibit renal clearance of methotrexate, leading to bone marrow toxicity, especially in the elderly or renal impaired.

value.effect: Aspirin may diminish the hypotensive and natriuretic response of ACE inhibitors via inhibition of renal prostaglandins.
value.management: Monitor blood pressure and renal function when aspirin is coadministered with ACE inhibitors.

refs.quote: The hyponatremic and hypotensive effects of ACE inhibitors may be diminished by the concomitant administration of aspirin due to its indirect effect on the renin-angiotensin conversion pathway.
Patients on anticoagulation therapy are at increased risk for bleeding because of drug-drug interactions and the effect on platelets.
